name: openturns
desc: Probabilistic modelling and uncertainty quantification library
why: Uncertainty quantification and probabilistic modelling is a real, under-explored scientific toolkit.

brief.what_it_is: OpenTURNS is a scientific library with C++ and Python interfaces for treating uncertainties. It provides an internal data model and algorithms for probabilistic modelling and uncertainty quantification. You feed it probability distributions, random variables, and models, and it returns statistical results such as distributions, sensitivity measures, and reliability estimates. The README describes the aim as supplying all the functionality needed for uncertainty studies with industrial applications. The README does not list specific algorithms, so those details are not confirmed from the sources I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the goal is to give engineers the tools to add a probabilistic dimension to studies that are currently deterministic. It is aimed at industrial applications.

commands_seen.context: Installs the Python binary package from PyPI. The install page says pip does not install pre-releases unless --pre is given.
Installs from conda-forge after Miniforge is set up. The page warns that conda may be slow or fail on complex environments.
Installs the Python module on Debian/Ubuntu after adding the OpenTURNS apt repository and signing key.
Installs the package on FreeBSD from FreshPorts.
Builds and installs the library through the Spack package manager.
Installs the C++ library from vcpkg.
Opens a NixOS shell that provides openturns.
Installs the Python package on Guix.
Installs the library under MSYS2 for the x86_64 MinGW-w64 flavour. Other flavours (ucrt, clang, clang-aarch64) are listed on the same page.
Installs the weekly nightly Python build. The page says to use it at your own risk.

brief.install_notes: Binary installs are available from PyPI, conda-forge (use Miniforge, not Anaconda's default channel), apt (OpenTURNS repository with a signing key), RPM repositories for Fedora, openSUSE and Mageia, and the Arch AUR, FreeBSD, NixOS, Spack, Guix, vcpkg and MSYS2. Source builds are documented separately under the library development section. The Homebrew install was not checked, and this brief does not confirm it. No hardware or account is needed. Python is required for the Python module.
brief.standout: The project covers a large range of uncertainty and risk methods in one library with a C++ core and Python bindings, aimed at engineers rather than statisticians. Its install page lists packaging for many distributions and package managers, which suggests it is meant for practical use in industry.
brief.status: Maintained, based on the docs. The install page is for version 1.27 and shows 'Last updated on Apr 27, 2026' with a copyright range through 2026. The README has no release date and I did not check the commit history or release tags.
brief.caveats: The README is short and does not list features, so the scope in what_it_is comes from the description, not a feature list. Licence is LGPL-3.0-or-later, and some parts have additional licences (see the LICENSE file and other COPYING files). Conda users must use conda-forge; the page says the packages do not work on top of Anaconda. The README says backwards compatibility is not always kept, and breaks are marked in the ChangeLog. Symbolic differentiation uses a modified copy of Ev3, a separate library, so that code has its own provenance.
quotes: OpenTURNS is a scientific C++ and Python library featuring an internal data model and algorithms dedicated to the treatment of uncertainties.
Targeted users are all engineers who want to introduce the probabilistic dimension in their so far deterministic studies.
OpenTURNS is free software distributed under the GNU Lesser General Public License version 3 or, at your option, any later version.

judge.reason: A substantial, relatively under-the-radar scientific toolkit that lets engineers turn deterministic models into probabilistic risk and uncertainty studies.

entry.title: OpenTURNS
entry.tldr: A C++ and Python library for uncertainty quantification: give it distributions and a model, get back sensitivities, reliability estimates and output distributions.
entry.deeper_look:
OpenTURNS is a scientific library for treating uncertainty. You describe inputs as probability distributions and random variables, wrap a model of your system, and the library returns statistical results: distributions of outputs, sensitivity measures, and reliability estimates. It has a C++ core and Python bindings. It installs no command-line executables, so you use it from Python.

The stated reason it exists is practical. In the project's words, "Targeted users are all engineers who want to introduce the probabilistic dimension in their so far deterministic studies." Many engineering calculations return one number from one set of inputs. Real inputs are never exact, so the question becomes how much the answer moves when they wobble, and how likely failure is.

That shift, from a single answer to a distribution of answers, is the door into a large field: uncertainty propagation, sensitivity analysis, and reliability analysis. The library is aimed at industrial use rather than statisticians. The README is short and does not list specific algorithms, so the documentation is where to find out what it covers.

The project is free software under LGPL-3.0-or-later. The README warns that backwards compatibility is not always kept, and that breaks are marked in the ChangeLog.
entry.install:
brew install openturns
# Python is required for the Python module. Other routes from the install page: pip3 install openturns, or conda install -y openturns (conda-forge via Miniforge, not Anaconda's default channel). No hardware or account needed. The Homebrew install was not checked in the brief.

try_this.what_happens: Installs the Python binary package from PyPI, a quick way to get the Python module if you want to skip Homebrew.
Opens a Nix shell that provides OpenTURNS without touching your main environment.

entry.whats_unique: It covers a wide range of uncertainty and risk methods in one library, with a C++ core and Python bindings, aimed at engineers rather than statisticians.
entry.caveats: The README is short and lists no features, and backwards compatibility is not always kept between versions, so check the docs for the version you install.
